Introduction to Data Science · University of Science, VNU-HCM (HCMUS)

This report documents the available progress through Milestone 1 — Crawling, using the supplied my_data benchmark exports. The report follows the structure of the provided example, but all project-specific figures below are based on the supplied data rather than the example’s corpus.

Milestone 1 — Crawling: discovery coverage, version downloads, LaTeX availability, metadata and reference collection, data-size changes, and measurement limitations.

The supplied summary.json identifies itself as a report-only export (report_only: true, measured: false). Therefore, its saved corpus statistics are useful for describing the existing output, but its 12.19-second wall-time field is not a fresh end-to-end crawling benchmark. Discovery is recorded as 0 seconds, no single-paper trial was recorded, and memory/disk peak measurements are absent. These missing measurements are reported as unavailable, not as zero.

The data indicates strong coverage for discovery and publication metadata. It also shows why download success and usable LaTeX coverage are different: some versions are PDF-only or have errors, so not every discovered paper can provide TeX for later parsing. Reference metadata completeness is reported for the saved arXiv-linked references; it should not be interpreted as proof that every reference in every bibliography was retained.

The numerical evidence in this report comes from my_data/summary.json and my_data/papers.csv supplied for this task. The CSV contains 5,000 publication rows and records per-paper version counts, download/TeX status, metadata and reference counts, and file sizes. The companion chapter gives definitions and caveats for the headline figures.

For the course requirements and audit baseline, consult the 

official Milestone 1 specification.

records.content:
Milestone 1 collects scientific papers from arXiv. Its goals are:

Resolve the arXiv IDs of the assigned range into papers and find every version of each paper.

Download the full-text LaTeX sources of every version (not the PDFs).

Crawl the metadata of each paper and the reference information of each paper through Semantic Scholar.

Keep the download state of every item so that the crawl can be resumed and audited.

Prepare the working corpus that Milestone 2 (parsing) and Milestone 3 (matching) consume.

All numbers and figures on this page are generated while the book is compiled, from the small result files in m1_data/
(summary.json, papers.csv, samples.csv) produced by the benchmark script.

import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import display, Markdown
import report_utils as ru

S = ru.load_json("m1_data/summary.json")
papers = ru.load_csv("m1_data/papers.csv")
samples = ru.load_csv("m1_data/samples.csv")
R, T, M, K, D = (S.get(k) or {} for k in ("run", "timing", "memory", "disk", "data"))



Warning

This is a report-only snapshot, exported on 28 October 2026. Counts describe the saved corpus, not a new crawl performed for this book. The stored 2,445.05 seconds come from a resumed pipeline run on 27 October: discovery was skipped and the references step exited with code 1. This is not a cold-start end-to-end benchmark. There are no RAM samples, peak RAM or peak temporary-disk measurements. Missing measurements are shown as “Not measured”.

Audit baseline: 

official Milestone 1 specification.

args = R.get("args") or {}
display(ru.kv_table([
    ("Prefix", args.get("prefix")),
    ("Start ID", args.get("start")),
    ("End ID", args.get("end")),

]))

The crawler is a sequence of independent programs, run end to end by a driver script (main.py):

Step

Program

What it does

discover

discover.py

Resolves the assigned IDs through the arXiv API, keeps the IDs that exist and reads the number of versions of each paper from the version suffix of the latest identifier.

download

download_sources.py

Downloads and extracts the source archive of each version individually.

clean

process_sources.py

Historical cleanup removed recognised binary figures while retaining other resources. Corrected tar/ZIP extraction admits only .tex and .bib before writing; original TeX bytes are preserved. LaTeX figure commands (figure environments, \includegraphics) stay untouched in the TeX files.

metadata

metadata.py

Writes publication-level metadata.json: title, authors, submission and revision dates. Corrected code preserves venue/journal references when supplied and writes actual versioned snapshots with explicit provenance; historical exports remain unchanged.

references

references.py

Writes references.json for each paper from the Semantic Scholar API.

Every step skips the work it has already done, so an interrupted run is simply started again. The driver records
the duration of each step in timings.json, and a step that fails stops the run with a non-zero exit code.
The discovery step is skipped automatically when discovery.json is already complete for the requested range.

A version whose source is not TeX (PDF only, another format, or an archive without .tex) is kept as an empty record instead of being dropped,
so coverage statistics reflect reality. The download status of each version is stored in download_status.json.

arXiv API through the arxiv Python client, using the modern client.results(search) style. The client enforces a delay of 3 seconds between calls,
in line with the API etiquette, and requests go through one connection at a time with a descriptive User-Agent.

Semantic Scholar Graph API through requests, with a free API key (read from the S2_API_KEY environment variable).

psutil for the performance measurements (RAM sampling of the whole process tree).

For every paper, the Semantic Scholar record is requested with the fields paperId, title, authors, year, externalIds, publicationDate and venue of each reference.

Papers are queried in batches (the batch endpoint, 50 papers per request), which keeps the number of requests low and avoids rate limiting.

A reference becomes a row of the references table only if externalIds contains an ArXiv key. Its identifier is normalised to the yymm-id form;
old-style identifiers published before 2007 (for example hep-th/9901001) are kept as they are.

The current code supports non-arXiv references by default, but this does not establish preservation in the existing corpus. Its resume logic skips completed reference files; see the read-only corpus audit below for actual retained rows.

The submission date of a reference with an arXiv ID is read from the arXiv API (the date of version 1), in batches of 100 IDs with a persistent cache.
If arXiv does not return the paper, the publicationDate of Semantic Scholar is used instead.

HTTP 429 and server errors are retried with exponential backoff that honours the Retry-After header. An invalid API key (HTTP 401/403) stops the program with a clear message
instead of marking every paper as failed.

One working folder per paper is created under data/:data/
|-- discovery.json            # resolved IDs and version lists
|-- download_status.json      # status of every version
|-- metadata_status.json
|-- references_status.json
|-- timings.json
`-- 2607-03694/               # one folder per publication
    |-- v1/, v2/, ...         # .tex and .bib files of each version
    |-- metadata.json
    `-- references.json

The folder layout above is supported by download_sources.py and the version-directory resolver in parse.py.

The 

official-requirements audit records unmet source-only extraction, venue and per-version provenance requirements. A single publication-level metadata/reference file is not evidence of a separate snapshot for every version. Non-arXiv reference preservation must be assessed from the retained data, not from the current crawler’s defaults.

error – the download failed and will be retried by the next run.

Download errors are version-level outcomes, whereas the overall success rate is publication-level. Several errors may belong to one publication. PDF-only and no-TeX versions count as completed download attempts but do not provide parsable TeX. A missing Semantic Scholar record is an explicit completed lookup, not a paper with verified reference coverage. The 100% reference-metadata score applies only to saved arXiv-linked references and does not establish completeness of all bibliographies.

The saved average number of references is larger than the saved arXiv-linked subset. The current crawler can retain non-arXiv references too; the equality of saved-reference and arXiv-reference averages in this snapshot must not be interpreted as proof that every returned reference was retained.

The benchmark’s final_corpus_bytes sums all files under discovered publication folders, including metadata, references and any other outputs present at export time; it is not a measurement restricted to .tex and .bib. Filesystem-wide peak extra usage, if sampled, would also differ from an absolute corpus peak. Here that peak was not measured.

RAM is the total memory of the whole process tree (the driver and every program it starts), sampled periodically.

Milestone 2 turns the raw LaTeX sources crawled in Milestone 1 into structured data:

Gather the files that are really part of each compilation, version by version.

Build a hierarchical tree of every version (document, sections, sentences, block formulas, figures, lists).

Standardize the content: LaTeX cleanup and math normalization.

Extract the references into BibTeX entries.

Deduplicate reference entries and full-text content across the versions of a publication.

Measure the success rate, running time, memory footprint and output size of the parser.

All numbers and figures on this page are generated while the book is compiled, from the small result files in m2_data/
(summary.json, papers.csv, samples.csv, tables_stats.json, kind_counts.json, failures.json, example.json).

import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import display, Markdown
import report_utils as ru

S = ru.load_json("m2_data/summary.json")
papers = ru.load_csv("m2_data/papers.csv")
samples = ru.load_csv("m2_data/samples.csv")
tables = ru.load_json("m2_data/tables_stats.json")
kinds = ru.load_json("m2_data/kind_counts.json")
failures = ru.load_json("m2_data/failures.json")
example = ru.load_json("m2_data/example.json")
R, T, M, O, D = (S.get(k) or {} for k in ("run", "timing", "memory", "output", "data"))



Note

The parser benchmark was measured on 2 November 2026 (run.measured: true). A publication with status ok means its processing job completed; individual versions can still be empty or failed. Publication completion and version parsing success use different denominators.

Audit baseline: 

official Milestone 2 specification.

Multi-file gathering. For every version, all .tex files are read and their comments are stripped first (an unescaped % starts a comment),
so a commented-out \input is treated as plain text and never followed. The publication root is the file that contains \documentclass
(and \begin{document}) and is not included by another file. \input, \include and \subfile are then expanded recursively, with a cycle and depth guard.
Every file that is not reachable from the root is a redundant auxiliary file and is ignored, so the parse follows the selected compilation tree. This heuristic does not guarantee equivalence to a compiled PDF: unresolved includes are omitted and author macros are not expanded.

Hierarchy construction. Inside \begin{document}...\end{document} a block scanner finds sectioning commands, environments and display math.
The sectioning commands that actually occur in a paper are ranked (part < chapter < section < subsection < subsubsection < paragraph < subparagraph)
and mapped to consecutive levels, so the level of every heading is detected automatically: a paper that only uses \section and \subsubsection gets two heading levels.
The abstract becomes an Abstract heading; unnumbered sections such as Acknowledgements and the appendices are kept;
the References section and the thebibliography environment are excluded.

Leaf elements. The leaves of the tree are:

sentences – the prose of body text;

block formulas – the contents of equation, align, gather, multline, eqnarray, $$...$$ and \[...\];

figures – figure and table environments (a table is a kind of figure here) and stand-alone tabular, algorithm and similar floats.
The LaTeX commands that define a figure (\includegraphics, \caption) are kept in the content.

itemize, enumerate and description become a list node whose item children contain their own sentences, formulas and figures; lists can be nested.

Sentence splitting. Text is split into paragraphs on blank lines and then into sentences at ., ? or ! followed by whitespace and a capital letter, a backslash, a dollar sign or a quote.
A dot never splits a sentence inside mathematics or inside command arguments (\cite, \url, \footnote), after common abbreviations (e.g., i.e., Fig., Eq., et al.),
after single-letter initials, or inside decimal numbers.

Versions without TeX. A version stored as an empty record by Milestone 1 (PDF only, other formats) is recorded with the status empty and produces no elements,
so the coverage statistics and the tables reflect reality.

Cleanup. Formatting commands without semantic content are removed (\centering, \midrule, \toprule, \hline, \vspace, \label, font-size and font-style switches, …),
as is the float placement option such as [htbp]. Style wrappers such as \textbf{x} and \emph{x} are unwrapped in prose, and whitespace is normalized, so that
formatting differences do not make identical texts look different.

Math normalization. All inline mathematics (\(...\), $...$) is written as $...$. All block mathematics ($$...$$, \[...\], equation, align, gather, multline, eqnarray)
is written as \begin{equation}...\end{equation}; multi-line environments are wrapped in aligned or gathered inside it, so the result stays valid LaTeX. \label and \nonumber are dropped.

Reference extraction. Citations defined with \bibitem are converted to BibTeX entries with regular expressions: \newblock segments, a quoted title, or sentence splitting
give the authors, title and venue, while the DOI, URL and year are matched separately; the entry type is inferred from the venue. The .bib files referenced by
\bibliography are read by a small brace-aware parser. Each entry has a citation key, entry type, title, authors, year, DOI, journal and URL.

Reference deduplication. The entries of all versions of a publication (and the entries inside one version) are grouped with a union-find structure:
two entries are the same reference when they share a DOI, a normalized title, or a citation key with a compatible title.
One citation key is chosen for each group (the most frequent one, the newest version on ties), the \cite{} commands that use the dropped keys are renamed, and the fields of
the duplicates are unionized by field: the newest non-empty value wins, and missing fields fall back to older entries. This does not concatenate conflicting author lists. A non-misc entry type takes priority over misc, even from an older version. Long normalized titles match without a year constraint; short non-empty titles require a year. The historical extraction used setdefault and could discard later fields under the same key. The corrected merge_bib_entry combines non-empty fields before cross-version unionization and retains conflicting values in bib_field_conflicts. These code fixes have not been applied to the historical corpus exports.

Full-text deduplication. After the \cite renaming, the identity of an element is its kind together with its cleaned text. Elements that match exactly across versions share one
element_id in the elements table, and the hierarchy table holds one node-parent edge per version. Repeated identical text inside a single version gets distinct ids,
so every version stays a tree.

Known limitations. Macros defined by the authors are not expanded, the \bibitem conversion is heuristic, and the text that follows a \paragraph{} heading belongs to that heading.

Publications are processed in parallel by a pool of worker processes, with a configurable per-publication alarm on platforms supporting SIGALRM. This timeout is not enforced by that mechanism on Windows, where this benchmark was measured. The status of each publication is saved periodically, so an interrupted run
resumes where it stopped.

Table

Columns

elements

element_id, arxiv_id, kind, content

hierarchy

arxiv_id, version, element_id, parent_id

bibtex

arxiv_id, citation_key, entry_type, title, authors, year, doi, journal, url

Element ids start with the publication key, followed by a discriminant that is unique inside the publication (for example 2310-12345#s1).

]))
ru.bar(list(kinds), {"Elements": list(kinds.values())}, "Elements by kind", "Number of elements", log_y=True)

The element ids that appear in several versions are the result of full-text deduplication: one element row serves every version, while the hierarchy rows attach it to a parent of each version.

The running time is the end-to-end wall time of the parser. The memory is the total RAM of the whole process tree (the main process and all its workers), sampled periodically.

The current measured run is Windows-only. No Google Colab CPU-only parser runtime, peak RAM or final storage measurement has been collected. 

Colab benchmark protocol keeps those future runs separate.

display(ru.kv_table([
    ("Platform", R.get("platform")),
    ("Python", R.get("python")),
    ("CPU cores", R.get("cpu_count")),
    ("Measured at", R.get("created_at")),
    ("Measured run (not report-only)", R.get("measured")),
]))

The worker-time column is elapsed time inside a worker, despite the summary field name avg_seconds_per_paper_cpu; it is not an operating-system CPU-time measurement. Parallel workers make its average different from wall time divided by publication count. Summed process-tree RSS may count shared memory more than once. Samples are taken periodically, so short-lived peaks may be missed.

Per-publication parsed.json files and merged JSONL tables are alternative representations of the same results. Their sizes are reported separately; neither is the size of the original downloaded corpus. The 331 empty versions include 17 missing source directories, not only PDF-only papers. The two no_root_file failures remain visible above. Exact-text deduplication does not detect paraphrases or semantic equivalence; bibliography merging remains heuristic.

The benchmark invokes parse.py without --export, so merged-table generation is not included in its wall time. The reported merged-table sizes describe existing artifacts; the summary alone does not establish when those tables were regenerated. Root-cause inspection of the two failures and executable checks of deduplication are in the 

evidence audit. These checks do not change historical results or prove every parsed sentence correct.
